passage: Sit down, Ishita, you keep asking how your Dadi and I said yes to each other. I am Shankar, and I was a young man of twenty-one with one good shirt. My father showed me a photograph and I agreed only to meet her. We sat in her uncle's front room in Nashik, both families on the sofas, the tea far too sweet. Her father asked about my wages. Your Dadi, Lata, asked what I thought of a wife who kept teaching. Her mother's face tightened, but Lata's eyes stayed on me. Afterwards I told my father, "I like her, but she decides freely, and I will wait even for a no." She asked for three days and one more meeting, on the verandah with the door open. I kept checking the gate all three days, hoping, and telling myself a no would be hers to give. On the fifth day she said yes.

qa.q: Where did the two families meet?
qa.a: They met in Lata's uncle's front room in Nashik, with both families on the sofas.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling during the three days of waiting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Shankar was hopeful but nervous. He kept checking the gate while telling himself a no would be Lata's to give.

qa.q: Which choice by young Shankar kept the match from being rushed?
qa.a: He told his father that Lata decides freely and that he would wait even for a no, which gave her three days and another meeting.

qa.q: How might Lata have felt when Shankar said he would accept a no?
qa.a: Probably relieved and more trusting, since she could answer honestly without fear of anger.

grounding: A young adult takes part in an arranged match, meets the other person with both families present, and both keep the freedom to refuse.

passage: The power cut came ten minutes into the meeting, and monsoon rain hammered the tin awning over the Nagpur flat. Kavitha, twenty-one, sat in the candlelit hall with her parents on one side and Vikram's parents on the other. The visitors' train left at nine. Vikram's sister Sarika lit a second candle and whispered, "Ask him everything, we haven't got long." Kavitha did: would he mind her keeping her teaching post, who cooked at his house, what he did when he was angry. Vikram answered without glancing at his parents. When the taxi honked outside, Kavitha said, "I'd like to meet once more, just the two of us over chai, before I say yes or no." "And if it's no, that's an honest answer," Vikram said. Both mothers, surprised, nodded.

qa.q: What happened ten minutes into the meeting?
qa.a: The power cut came, and monsoon rain hammered the tin awning over the Nagpur flat.

qa.q: What might Kavitha be feeling as she asks about her teaching post and his temper?
qa.a: She is determined and serious, wanting to know the real person before deciding. She is probably a little nervous too, but she spends the short time on questions rather than politeness.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make when the taxi honked, and why did it help?
qa.a: She asked for a second meeting, just the two of them, before answering. It gave time and a chance to talk freely, and let both say plainly whether they want to go on.

qa.q: How does Vikram seem to see Kavitha's request for another meeting?
qa.a: He accepts it calmly and treats a no as an honest answer, so he sees the match as a decision for both of them.

grounding: A young adult meets a prospective partner with both families present and asks for more time, keeping the right to say no.

passage:
The first time I met Chandrika, our parents sat on one sofa and we sat on two chairs that faced each other like a job interview. Her father asked about my salary. My mother asked whether she cooked. I wanted to disappear.
Then Chandrika said, "Omkar, can we two go for a walk? Just around the park." Her mother hesitated, then nodded.
Outside, she asked me what I did on bad days. I told her I clean the whole kitchen. She laughed and said she sleeps for ten hours. We talked about her plan to finish her law degree, and about my father's health, which worries me.
Walking back, she said, "If either of us says no after a few meetings, can we promise the families won't take it as an insult?" I said yes. That promise made me want to meet her again.

qa.q: What does Omkar say he does on bad days?
qa.a: Omkar says he cleans the whole kitchen on bad days.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when their parents sat facing each other on the sofa?
qa.a: Omkar felt awkward and embarrassed, as if in a job interview; he says he wanted to disappear when the questions were about salary and cooking.

qa.q: Which choice made the meeting work better, and why?
qa.a: Chandrika's request for a walk, and the promise that either of them could say no, turned the meeting into a real conversation between two people who both kept a choice.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's mother see the request for a walk?
qa.a: She hesitates, so she may feel a little uneasy about tradition or what others think, but by nodding she shows she trusts her daughter to get to know Omkar herself.

grounding: It shows a young adult in an arranged match meeting the person and both families, where the search is shared and both keep a real right to say no.

passage:
Pre-marriage conversation session, community centre, Saturday.
Aadhya and Gautam came with both mothers for their second meeting. The families had already exchanged horoscopes and were keen. I asked each person to write three things they wanted in a home life, then read them aloud.
Aadhya wrote: time for her music, living near her parents for a few years, sharing chores. Gautam wrote: a quiet home, a dog, and room to change jobs. Both mothers laughed at the dog.
When I asked, "What would make you say no?" Gautam's mother began answering for him. Gautam touched her arm and answered himself: "If one of us felt we couldn't say no." Aadhya looked at him for a long moment and smiled.
Next step: I suggested two more meetings without the mothers, in a café, and asked both families to agree that either answer is acceptable. Both agreed.

qa.q: What three things did Gautam write?
qa.a: Gautam wrote: a quiet home, a dog, and room to change jobs.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's long look and smile suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt relieved and reassured, because Gautam's answer showed he also wanted both of them to keep the freedom to say no.

qa.q: Why was it wise to suggest meetings without the mothers?
qa.a: It gives Aadhya and Gautam space to speak for themselves, as Gautam had to when his mother began answering for him, and to decide freely.

qa.q: How does the note-writer help the families see the match?
qa.a: By asking both families to accept either answer, the note-writer turns the match into a shared search in which Aadhya and Gautam each keep a genuine choice.

grounding: It shows a young couple in an arranged match meeting and talking with both families, where each keeps a real right to refuse.

passage:
Thursday night
Met him today. Phuppo's friend's nephew. We sat in their drawing room with rose sherbet while five adults pretended not to listen.
He was nervous too, which helped! He asked if I still wanted to do my master's. I said yes, in Hyderabad. He said, "Good. I'd rather marry someone who's doing what she wants." I didn't know what to say, so I asked about his cricket team.
Then Ammi asked, in front of everyone, "So Noor, what do you think?" I froze. He said quickly, "Aunty, we should talk a few more times first." I could have hugged him. (I didn't.)
Called Rukmini after. She asked, "Do you like him?" Honestly? Not sure yet. But I liked that nobody made me answer tonight. Meeting two, maybe next week. 🙂

qa.q: What did Noor say she wanted to do?
qa.a: Noor said yes, she still wanted to do her master's, in Hyderabad.

qa.q: How can you tell Noor felt relieved when he answered Ammi?
qa.a: She writes that she froze when Ammi asked, and then says she could have hugged him when he asked for a few more talks first; she felt relieved and grateful not to be pushed into an answer.

qa.q: What could Noor do before the second meeting?
qa.a: She could write down a few questions that matter to her, about her studies, where they would live and how they share decisions, so the next talk goes beyond polite chat.

qa.q: What might Rukmini be hoping when she asks whether Noor likes him?
qa.a: As Noor's friend, Rukmini probably wants to know how Noor herself feels, apart from the families, and hopes Noor is choosing freely.

grounding: It shows a young adult taking part in an arranged meeting as a shared search, keeping the right to take time and to say no.
